core.text: Which tense of the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do) goes inside an *ut*, *nē*, *cum* or question clause depends on the main verb. That pairing is **the sequence of tenses (a present main verb takes the present subjunctive, a past one the imperfect)**: *imperat ut veniās* (he orders you to come) but *imperāvit ut venīrēs* (he ordered you to come). Latin name: *cōnsecūtiō temporum*.
English shifts too: he says he *is* coming; he said he *was* coming.

Main verb present or future → the present subjunctive (the 'may / let' form: veniat = let him come, may he come); main verb imperfect, perfect or pluperfect → the imperfect subjunctive. The same rule covers purpose, result, indirect command, cum clauses and indirect questions.

invented.la: Rogat ut maneam. — Rogāvit ut manērem.
invented.en: He asks me to stay. — He asked me to stay.

core.text: The imperfect subjunctive (the past-time 'might / would' form: veniret; built on the infinitive) is not 'past meaning' but 'past setting': in *vēnit ut vidēret* the seeing is still ahead from his point of view. Choose the tense by the main verb, then translate the clause naturally ('to see', 'to stay').

more.text: The learner's notes list five dependent uses and shift each one: *imperō / imperābō ut veniās* but *imperāvī ut venīrēs*; *veniō ut doceam* but *vēnī ut docērem*; *ita clāmō ut proximōs suscitem* but *clāmāvī ut suscitārem*; *bibō cum sitiam* (I drink because I am thirsty) but *bibēbam cum sitīrem*; *nesciō quid videam* but *nesciēbam quid vidērem*.

Two more tenses fill in 'already finished': after a present main verb the perfect subjunctive (Week 10: *nesciō quid fēcerit*, I don't know what he did), after a past main verb the pluperfect subjunctive (Week 12: *nesciēbam quid fēcisset*). So each main-verb group has a 'same time' tense and a 'before' tense.

In a present-tense story (the historic present) a writer may still use the imperfect: *rogat ut manēret*; the story is past even if the verb is present. Ørberg's chapter 28 drills the pair with *monet ut pāreat* / *monēbat, monuit ut pārēret*; chapter 29 sets *tempus praesēns* against *tempus praeteritum* for purpose and result alike.

teach.title: The main verb decides
teach.say: Which tense of the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do) goes inside an *ut*, *nē* or *cum* clause is not left to you: the verb in the main clause (the sentence's own verb, not one tucked inside another clause) fixes it. That pairing is **the sequence of tenses (a present main verb takes the present subjunctive, a past one the imperfect)**. *Imperat ut veniat* against *imperāvit ut venīret*: change one word in the main clause and the other clause has to change too.

check.ask: Which tense of the subjunctive is venīret?

teach.title: Present and future take the present subjunctive
teach.say: A main verb in the present takes the present subjunctive after it — and the future counts on the same side: *currit ut vocet*, *mittet ut arent*. So read the main verb first, satisfy yourself that it is not past, and write the present subjunctive: *vocet*, *arent*, *currant*.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form of currō that ōrat calls for.

teach.title: Any past tense takes the imperfect subjunctive
teach.say: A main verb in a past tense takes the imperfect subjunctive (the past-time 'might / would' form: venīret; built on the infinitive): *cucurrit ut vocāret*, *ōrāvit nē currerent*. This does not mean the clause happened earlier — in *cucurrit ut vocāret* the calling is still ahead of the running. It means only that the whole scene sits in the past.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form of currō that ōrāvit calls for.

teach.title: The same rule in every kind of clause
teach.say: The rule is not about *ut*. It holds for purpose, for result, for *cum* clauses and for indirect questions alike: *tam fessus est ut dormiat* against *tam fessus erat ut dormīret*; *quaerit ubi sit* against *quaesīvit ubi esset*. Whatever the clause, find the main verb and let it choose.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form of sum that quaesīvit calls for.

teach.title: Every past tense counts as past
teach.say: 'Past' here means the imperfect, the perfect and the pluperfect all together: *legēbat*, *lēgit* and *lēgerat* every one of them call for the imperfect subjunctive. Only the present and the future sit on the other side. So when the main verb is *tacēbat*, the *nē* clause takes *audīret*, not *audiat*.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form of audiō that tacēbat calls for.
